newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish Life says new business up 42 pct in 96.
newsitem.headline: Irish Life says new business up 42 pct in 96.

text.p: Irish Life Plc said on Thursday that the value of new business increased by 42 percent in 1996 while total sales across the group rose by three percent to 108 million Irish pounds on an annual weighted premium equivalent basis.
But sales slipped by over three percent to 444.0 million Irish pounds when the full value of both single and recurring premiums was taken into account.
Overall operating profit rose by nine percent to 93 million punts.

Total sales in Ireland increased by 11 percent to 71.4 million Irish pounds and this, along with a strong sales performance by Irish Life International, countered a decline in U.S. sales because of the general underperformance of the U.S. fixed annuity market in 1996, Irish Life said.
It said its associated businesses had another good year in 1996.

Irish Intercontinental Bank, in which the group has a 25 percent interest, achieved another year of profit growth while Irish Life Finance Group, where Irish Life has an effective 50 percent interest, reported a 29 percent rise in total advances to 236 million.
Irish Life's 30 percent-owned general insurance affiliate, AGF-Irish Life Holdings, also increased turnover and operating profit in a very competitive market.

The company said its corporate division had another successful year with total sales rising by 17.3 percent to 91.4 million, reflecting its continued success in the annuity market where sales reached 55 million.
Irish Life said all its funds enjoyed a good performance on the back of strong markets in 1996.

Investment earnings rose to 20.7 million Irish pounds from 17.1 million a year earlier, boosted by strong stock markets as well as an exceptional gain on a property disposal in the first half of the year.

On a geographical basis, Irish Life said its U.S. operations showed an improved profit performance last year with product and investment earnings of $19.1 million, up from $14.7 million a year earlier.

In Britain, earnings slipped to 11.5 million sterling from 16.1 million but the 1995 outcome benefited from once-off expense reserve releases as the appointed representative distribution business was closed down.
The UK outcome reflected tight cost management of the existing book of business and a positive new business contribution from premium indexations and top-ups, the group said.

Irish Life International, the joint venture operating from Dublin's International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) reported a rise in sales to 47.8 million sterling from 14.2 million in its second full year of operation.
Irish Life's French subsidiary, Xaar, achieved a 20 percent increase in sales to 69.2 million French francs but volumes at this level are short of the level required to meet overheads.
The company focused on the smaller broker market in the latter half of 1996 and a number of direct selling outlets were closed as consequence.
"Other efforts at achieving critical mass have centred on seeking a suitable partner but to date these efforts have proved unsuccessful," Irish Life said.
